import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Number of digits of n raised to the power of the sum of the digits of n

*References:*
- [A113010](https://oeis.org/A113010)
-/

namespace OeisA113010

open Nat

/--
a n is the {Number of digits of n} raised to the power of {the sum of the digits of n}.
-/
def a (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((10).digits n).length ^ (List.sum ((10).digits n))

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_0 : a 0 = 1 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_1 : a 1 = 1 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_2 : a 2 = 1 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_3 : a 3 = 1 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_4 : a 4 = 1 := by native_decide

/--
$n=1$ and $32$ are two fixed points. Are there any others?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem conjecture : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n : ℕ, a n = n ∧ n > 0 → n = 1 ∨ n = 32 := by
  sorry

end OeisA113010

findings.description: The answer polarity is reversed. At line 55, the right-hand side says that there are no fixed points other than 1 and 32, whereas the source asks whether another fixed point exists. Thus completing the slot with answer(True) would give a negative answer to the source's question, and answer(False) would give a positive one. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, I proved that this right-hand side is equivalent to ¬(∃ n : ℕ, a n = n ∧ n ≠ 1 ∧ n ≠ 32), and is not equivalent to the existential itself, without using the sorry-backed conjecture.
findings.source_evidence: OEIS A113010, first comment: “n=1 and 32 are two fixed points. Are there any others?” Read in the official OEIS export at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A113/A113010.seq, corresponding to https://oeis.org/A113010.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the right-hand side with the existence statement: `theorem conjecture : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ n : ℕ, a n = n ∧ n ≠ 1 ∧ n ≠ 32 := by sorry`. An additional `0 < n` condition is harmless but unnecessary because `a 0 = 1`.

reformulations.difference: Nat.digits uses little-endian order and represents zero by [], unlike the source's Python decimal-string implementation, which represents zero by one digit.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Reversing the digits changes neither their length nor their sum. At zero, Lean computes 0^0 = 1, while the source computes 1^0 = 1. Consequently the complete function agrees at every natural number. The scratch file proves pointwise equality with the conventional decimal-digit definition using [0] at zero, and also proves equivalence of the resulting fixed-point predicates.

sources_consulted: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A113/A113010.seq — complete official export of the cited OEIS entry; direct access to https://oeis.org/A113010 returned HTTP 403.
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/README.md — provenance of the official OEIS export.

/opt/formal-conjectures/STATEMENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and AGENTS.md — review checklist and conventions.

/workspace/past_misformalizations/INDEX.md and pr01922.md, pr03406.md, pr03679.md, pr04987.md, pr05029.md, pr01191.md — historical calibration only.
review.notes: Checked all seven declarations. The five test theorems match the source. Lean also verified all 59 published sequence terms, a 32 = 32, and that the only fixed points below 10000 are 1 and 32. The positivity restriction in the conjecture is redundant, not a defect; this was proved separately. The current OEIS export records only the finite-search remark “There are no other fixed points less than 10^1000” (Chai Wah Wu, February 28, 2019), so it supplies no reason to change the research-open status. Experiments are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean and /workspace/review/computations.lean; both compile successfully.

submission.summary: Corrected the answer polarity by asking whether a fixed point distinct from 1 and 32 exists. All other declarations, docstrings, references, and attributes are unchanged. The required compile command succeeds with only the permitted `declaration uses sorry` warning.
